column2: Crop circles. A top-down view of a wheat field at night, the 2:1 strip a band of golden-green wheat whose stalks sway in travelling wind waves at 60 fps (a real wind field: gusts roll across, the light catches the bent heads, you can see individual ears at the near scale). The numerals are crop circles: wheat flattened in swirled patterns, with the flattened lay of the stalks shown as spiral grain (lighter, glossy, combed), standing edges crisp, the way real formations look from the air. Design all ten digits as formations: rings, swirls and paths, a 0 a flattened ring around a standing island, an 8 two interlocked swirl rings joined by a path. Minute turn: a small UFO hovers over the changing digit; its beam makes the old formation's stalks stand back up in a ripple (gone before :00), then it spins and lays the new formation in a sweeping spiral (after :00), stalks falling in order. Hour: a bigger show: the mothership arrives, the whole field lights up in a pattern that resolves into the new time, cows float up and are put down again. Day (sunlight, a farmer on a tractor, a scarecrow) and night (moonlight, beam glow) should both look designed. The UFO and any cow must be bold, simple and readable at --scale 4.

Harbin Ice and Snow Festival (哈尔滨冰雪大世界). The numerals are buildings of an ice-lantern palace: carved from translucent ice blocks, with brick courses, tiny crenellations, onion domes or pagoda roofs, lit from inside by coloured LEDs that slowly cycle (cyan, magenta, amber, green) so light glows through the ice, refracts at edges and shows bubbles and saw marks. Design all ten digit-buildings as a set, unmistakable as digits first. Night sky over a snowy plaza (deep indigo, not black, with fine snow falling in parallax at 60 fps), little bundled-up visitors with scarves walking past, a slide with sledders, breath steam. Minute turn: ice carvers with chainsaws (bold, 14+ px, with orange suits) cut the old digit's blocks away in a spray of ice chips, then a crane lowers fresh blocks that light up course by course into the new digit; the time is never wrong. Hour: a bigger show, e.g. the whole palace's lights run a chase in sequence, fireworks reflected in the ice, or the lights all switch to a new colour scheme in a wave. By day (the festival is a night thing, but the clock runs all day): pale blue-white ice in winter sun with sharp blue shadows; switch to the coloured lighting at dusk.

Oskar Schlemmer's Triadisches Ballett (Bauhaus, 1922). The numerals are dancers in Schlemmer's geometric costumes: each digit is one costumed figure whose padded discs, spirals, cones, hoops, wire skirts and masks make the digit's shape (a 0 the dancer with the round hoop skirt seen as a ring, a 1 the tall "Goldkugel" figure, a 8 two stacked discs), so they are numberfolk, characters first, with small masked heads, arms and feet. Design all ten as a set, legible and charming. They perform on a stage: a deep coloured backdrop (Bauhaus yellow, red, blue, black-grey acts) with spotlights tracking them and floor shadows, and they move all the time at 60 fps, mechanical, marionette-like: turning, stepping, bobbing, arms swinging, costumes spinning. Minute turn: the changing dancer bows and exits into the wings (gone before :00), the new dancer enters in a spotlight and strikes its pose (after :00); choreography eased, the time never wrong. Hour: a new act of the ballet: the backdrop colour changes (yellow, pink, black acts as in the original), the curtain sweeps, and all four dancers do a group figure, still readable. Typography for any title card in Bauhaus geometric lettering you draw (circle, square, triangle). Keep the stage colour deep and deliberate; LCD black is grey.

A Katamari Damacy-style rolling game, top-down-ish three-quarter view of a candy-coloured town or a kid's bedroom floor. The numerals are piles of everyday objects lying on the floor arranged in digit shapes: pencils, erasers, sweets, dice, toy cars, rubber ducks, coins, building blocks, each bold and colourful with a dark outline, drawn as a set of ten digit-arrangements that read clearly. A tiny prince (bold green, with his antenna head, 12+ px) rolls a lumpy sticky ball around, always alive at 60 fps, the ball visibly rotating with the stuck objects poking out and turning with it. Minute turn: the prince rolls the katamari over the old digit, the objects jump onto the ball one by one with a pop and the ball grows (gone before :00); then the King of All Cosmos (a big bold head with a crown and a rainbow, entering from the edge or sky) throws the new digit's objects down, they bounce and settle into place (after :00); time never wrong. Hour: the ball has grown huge; the King launches it into the sky where it becomes a star, sparkles, and the new hour is rained down. Use the game's palette: bright pastels, rainbow trails, chunky shapes. Make the rolling ball's rotation smooth: it is the showcase for 60 fps.
